content: Weight loss exceeding 5% of usual body weight within a 6-12 month period is considered pathologic. Weight loss can be either intentional or unintentional, with unintentional weight loss being more prevalent among elderly individuals. In patients over the age of 65, common causes of weight loss include malignancies (particularly those affecting the digestive system and non-hematologic cancers), dementia, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and polymyalgia rheumatica. Oral disorders may also contribute to weight loss in this age group. For individuals under the age of 65, the primary causes of weight loss are endocrine disorders, infections (such as tuberculosis and HIV), psychiatric conditions (including depression, anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive disorder), and hematologic malignancies. A detailed patient history, obtained either from the patient or a caregiver, is essential in identifying the underlying cause of weight loss. It is critical to first evaluate the patient’s access to food and their nutritional status. A comprehensive physical examination, including observing an elderly patient eating a meal, can provide valuable insights into potential neurocognitive dysfunctions. Laboratory investigations such as a complete blood count (CBC) and comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) offer a general overview of the patient’s condition. Follow-up is necessary to address known causes and identify any unknown contributors to weight loss. A multidisciplinary approach is recommended to ensure optimal management. Nutritional supplements may be appropriate in select cases but should complement regular meals rather than replace them. Life-Threatening Causes of Weight Loss: Life-threatening causes include conditions that, if untreated, may result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours. For example, electrolyte disturbances caused by malnutrition can lead to arrhythmias, which may be fatal if not promptly corrected. Common Causes of Weight Loss by Age Group: Age > 65 years: Malignancies (digestive and non-hematologic) Dementia Stroke Parkinson's disease Polymyalgia rheumatica Oral disorders Age < 65 years: Endocrine disorders Infections (e.g., tuberculosis, HIV) Psychiatric disorders (e.g., depression, anxiety, OCD) Hematologic malignancies Diagnosis and Management: Perform a thorough physical examination to identify the cause of weight loss. Assess the patient’s nutritional status and screen for depression. Evaluate serum electrolytes to detect potentially life-threatening abnormalities. Prevent further weight loss by recommending proper meals, supplements, and consulting a nutritionist. Treat the underlying cause of weight loss. Monitor medications prescribed for weight gain, particularly in elderly patients, for potential side effects. Prefer liquid nutritional supplements over solid ones and serve them separately from regular meals. Encourage physical activity and physical therapy. Do Not: Neglect an oral examination, especially in elderly patients. Rely solely on patient history in cases where cognitive dysfunction is present.
